title: Our Galaxy, the Milky Way
summary: What the Milky Way galaxy is, its spiral shape and black hole center, where our Sun sits in it, and why we see it as a band of light in dark skies.
poll: Everyone should get the chance to see the Milky Way in a dark sky.

versions.title: Our Home in Space
versions.text:
Look up at night. Do you see a band of light? It is soft and white. It is the Milky Way. It is our galaxy.

A galaxy is a huge group of stars. It has gas and dust, too. Our Sun is one of its stars. There are more than a hundred billion stars in it. That is a lot!

It is flat. It is round. It has long arms. The arms curl. So it is a spiral. Think of a pinwheel. We live in one arm. We are far from the center.

At the center is a black hole. It is so big. It pulls on all things near it. It all spins. Our Sun goes round it. One trip takes a long, long time.

Long ago, a man used a telescope. His name was Galileo. He saw the band. It was made of lots of stars.

In Arabic, the band has a name. It is Darb al-Tabbana. It means the path of the straw sellers.

Bright lights in towns hide it. Go to a dark place. In Saudi Arabia, the sand lands are dark at night. They are a great place to look. Bring a friend. Look up!

A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas, and dust. Our Sun is just one star in the Milky Way. It has more than a hundred billion stars!

The Milky Way is flat and round. It is like a plate. It has long arms that curl out. This shape is called a spiral. It looks like a pinwheel. Our Sun is in one of the arms. It is far from the center.

At the center is a giant black hole. It pulls hard on things near it. The whole galaxy turns. Our Sun goes around the center. One trip takes a very long time.

About four hundred years ago, a man named Galileo used a telescope. He looked at the band. He saw that it was made of lots and lots of stars.

In Arabic, the band is called Darb al-Tabbana. That means the path of the straw sellers.

Bright city lights hide the Milky Way. You need a dark place to see it. In Saudi Arabia, the desert sky is dark. It is a great place to look. Go with your family. Bring a warm coat. Then look up!

versions.title: The Milky Way: Our Spiral Home
versions.text:
On a dark, clear night far from city lights, you may notice a long band of soft, white light stretching across the sky, and that glowing band is the Milky Way, the galaxy we call home.

A galaxy is an enormous collection of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Our Sun is merely one ordinary star in the Milky Way, which astronomers estimate contains between one hundred billion and four hundred billion stars.

The Milky Way is shaped like a flat disk with a bulge in the middle, and long arms curl outward from its center, so astronomers classify it as a spiral galaxy that would resemble a gigantic pinwheel from a great distance. Its diameter is approximately 100,000 light-years, meaning a beam of light would require about one hundred thousand years to cross it. Our Sun is located in a minor arm, roughly halfway between the center and the edge.

At the center is a supermassive black hole, about four million times heavier than the Sun, whose gravity pulls on everything nearby. The entire galaxy gradually rotates, and our Sun follows an orbit around the center that takes more than two hundred million years to complete.

About four hundred years ago, the Italian scientist Galileo made careful observations of the band through a telescope and discovered that it was composed of countless faint stars.

The Milky Way is not alone, because astronomers estimate that the universe holds billions of other galaxies. The nearest large spiral, called Andromeda, lies about 2.5 million light-years away. Observers in very dark places can glimpse it as a faint smudge without a telescope.

In Arabic, the band is called Darb al-Tabbana, which means the path of the straw sellers.

Light pollution from cities conceals the Milky Way. It is difficult to observe from populated areas. In Saudi Arabia, the dark desert sky is one of the most spectacular places to view it.

versions.title: The Milky Way: Our Spiral Home
versions.text:
On a dark, clear night far from city lights, you may notice a long band of soft, white light stretching across the sky, and that glowing band is the Milky Way, the enormous galaxy that humanity calls home.

A galaxy is an immense collection of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, and our Sun is merely one ordinary star in the Milky Way, which astronomers estimate contains between one hundred billion and four hundred billion stars.

The Milky Way is shaped like a flattened disk with a bulge in the middle, and long arms curl outward from its center, so astronomers classify it as a spiral galaxy that would resemble a gigantic pinwheel from a tremendous distance. Its diameter is approximately 100,000 light-years, meaning a beam of light would require about one hundred thousand years to travel across it. A single light-year equals roughly 9.5 trillion kilometers, an almost unimaginable distance. Our Sun, meanwhile, is located in a relatively minor arm, roughly halfway between the center and the outer edge.

At the center is a supermassive black hole, approximately four million times heavier than the Sun, whose powerful gravity influences everything nearby. The entire galaxy gradually rotates, and our Sun follows an orbit around the center that requires more than two hundred million years to complete.

About four hundred years ago, the Italian scientist Galileo made careful observations of the band through a telescope and discovered that it was composed of countless faint stars that unaided human eyes cannot separate individually.

The Milky Way is certainly not alone, because astronomers estimate that the observable universe holds billions of other galaxies. The nearest large spiral, called Andromeda, lies approximately 2.5 million light-years away, and observers in exceptionally dark places can glimpse it as a faint, fuzzy smudge without any telescope at all.

In Arabic, the band is traditionally called Darb al-Tabbana, which means the path of the straw sellers.

Light pollution from illuminated cities conceals the Milky Way. It is difficult to observe from populated areas, but in Saudi Arabia, the dark desert sky is one of the most spectacular locations for viewing it.

versions.title: The Milky Way: Our Spiral Home
versions.text:
On a dark, clear night far from city lights, you may notice a long band of soft, white light stretching across the sky, and that glowing band is the Milky Way, the enormous galaxy that humanity calls home.

A galaxy is an immense collection of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, and our Sun is merely one ordinary star in the Milky Way, which astronomers estimate contains between one hundred billion and four hundred billion stars.

The Milky Way is shaped like a flattened disk with a bulge in the middle, and long arms curl outward from its center, so astronomers classify it as a spiral galaxy that would resemble a gigantic pinwheel from a tremendous distance. Its diameter is approximately 100,000 light-years, meaning a beam of light would require about one hundred thousand years to travel across it. A single light-year equals roughly 9.5 trillion kilometers, an almost unimaginable distance. Our Sun, meanwhile, is located in a relatively minor arm, roughly halfway between the center and the outer edge.

At the center is a supermassive black hole, approximately four million times heavier than the Sun, whose powerful gravity influences everything in its vicinity, including stars, clouds of gas, and dust. The entire galaxy gradually rotates, and our Sun follows an orbit around the center that requires more than two hundred million years to complete.

About four hundred years ago, the Italian scientist Galileo made careful observations of the band through a telescope and discovered, to the astonishment of many scholars, that it was composed of countless faint stars that unaided human eyes cannot distinguish individually.

The Milky Way is certainly not alone, because astronomers estimate that the observable universe contains billions of other galaxies. The nearest large spiral, called Andromeda, lies approximately 2.5 million light-years away, and observers in exceptionally dark locations can glimpse it as a faint, fuzzy smudge without any telescope at all.

In Arabic, the shimmering band across the night sky is traditionally called Darb al-Tabbana, which means the path of the straw sellers.

Light pollution from illuminated cities conceals the Milky Way. This makes it extremely difficult to observe from populated areas, but in Saudi Arabia, the dark desert sky provides one of the most spectacular locations for viewing it, especially on cool winter evenings when the air is dry and transparent.

HIGH.prompt: Describe the Milky Way to someone who has never heard of it. Include its shape, its size, what lies at its center, and why it can be hard to see.
checklist: I described the spiral shape and the diameter in light-years.
I explained the supermassive black hole at the center.
I explained how light pollution affects viewing the Milky Way.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a huge spiral-shaped collection of more than one hundred billion stars with a bulge in the middle and long curling arms, including the small arm where our own Sun sits. Astronomers estimate its diameter at about 100,000 light-years, meaning light itself takes that long to cross from one side to the other. At its very center lies a supermassive black hole whose powerful gravity controls how the whole galaxy slowly turns. Even though it fills the sky as a soft band of light, bright city lights create light pollution that can hide it completely, so clear observation of the Milky Way really only happens far from cities, such as in the dark desert skies of Saudi Arabia.
